A business model describes the rationale of how an organization creates, delivers, and captures value.

## Business Model Canvas and Sustainability-Oriented Extensions

Developing business models requires a theoretical framework that are developed in academia or buinsess. First

-   **2004**: Alexander Osterwalder introduces the Business Model Canvas.
-   **2010**: Business Model Generation book is published.
-   **2015**: Business Model Navigator book is published.

The traditional BMC (Osterwalder & Pigneur, 2010) is a strategic management tool that breaks a business model into 9 building blocks (value proposition, customers, channels, revenue streams, etc.). It focuses primarily on the *economic* logic of how an organization creates, delivers, and captures value. However, on its own the original BMC does not explicitly account for environmental or social impacts. Researchers have noted that **sustainability dimensions need additional consideration or modifications** to the BMC when it’s applied to NBS or eco-initiatives​[[mdpi.com]{.underline}](https://www.mdpi.com/2071-1050/15/19/14091#:~:text=already%20existing%20modifications%20of%20the,is%20divided%20into%20four%20steps). In other words, while the BMC is a great starting point, it requires extension to holistically describe NBS-focused models that generate public goods (e.g. biodiversity gains) alongside private benefits.

**Triple-Layered Business Model Canvas (TLBMC):** Joyce & Paquin (2016) introduced the TLBMC as a tool to design more sustainable business models by adding two new layers to the canvas​[[mdpi.com]{.underline}](https://www.mdpi.com/2071-1050/15/19/14091#:~:text=37,Layered). In this framework, **three aligned canvases** represent the **economic, environmental, and social** aspects of a business model. The **economic layer** is essentially the original 9-block BMC (covering value proposition, key partners, customers, cost structure, etc.). The **environmental layer** also uses nine blocks but centers on lifecycle and resource considerations – for example, **materials**, **production**, **distribution**, **use phase**, and **end-of-life** are considered to map the environmental footprint. The **social layer** likewise has nine blocks focusing on societal stakeholders and impacts – e.g. **social value**, **governance**, **employees**, **community**, and other social benefits. Importantly, the triple-layered approach ensures **vertical coherence** between layers: for MD DEMO, this means decisions in the economic model (e.g. offering sport-fishing tourism) are checked against environmental impacts (e.g. fish population dynamics, resource use) and social outcomes (e.g. community livelihoods, recreational benefits). The TLBMC’s comprehensive structure is highly relevant to MD DEMO as it forces consideration of how Green Hatcheries and tourism not only generate revenue but also how they reuse resources (like water, biomass) and involve local communities. In sum, the TLBMC helps embed **triple bottom line** thinking (economic, environmental, social) directly into business model design.

**Threebility – The Sustainable Business Model Canvas:** Developed by Gerlach (2015), “Threebility” is another integrated canvas tool designed to bring sustainability into core business model planning. Similar to the triple-layer concept, the Threebility approach emphasizes **economic, environmental, and socio-cultural aspects** on a single canvas. It modifies the BMC by placing greater emphasis on sustainability-related elements in each building block. For example, Threebility prompts consideration of not just customer value, but also **societal value propositions**, and it explicitly asks how operations reduce environmental harm or create social good. The goal is to provide a *“common language for sustainable innovation”* that any enterprise (or project like MD DEMO) can use to ideate greener models​[[mdpi.com]{.underline}](https://www.mdpi.com/2071-1050/15/19/14091#:~:text=8,innovation%20%28accessed%20on%2015). In practice, tools like the Threebility canvas offer **guiding questions** for each block focusing on sustainability – ensuring that MD DEMO’s plan for, say, regenerative tourism, addresses not only tourist satisfaction and revenue, but also educational value for visitors, habitat restoration contributions, and cultural significance for local people. By using such a canvas, MD DEMO can **incentivize innovative ideas** that align profitability with ecological regeneration.

**Nature-Based Business Model Canvas (proGIreg 2023):** Recent EU research has produced NBS-specific business model frameworks. A notable example is the **Nature-Based Sustainability Business Model Canvas (NB S BMC)** from the EU Horizon 2020 **proGIreg** project​[[econpapers.repec.org]{.underline}](https://econpapers.repec.org/RePEc:gam:jsusta:v:15:y:2023:i:19:p:14091-:d:1245905#:~:text=Abstract%3A%20Businesses%20are%20under%20pressure,capture%20the%20core%20concepts%20of)​[[econpapers.repec.org]{.underline}](https://econpapers.repec.org/RePEc:gam:jsusta:v:15:y:2023:i:19:p:14091-:d:1245905#:~:text=NBS,It%20consists%20of%2014%20building). Stork *et al.* (2023) conducted an extensive literature review of BMC modifications and then **designed a new canvas tailored to NBS**, tested in three living lab cities​[[econpapers.repec.org]{.underline}](https://econpapers.repec.org/RePEc:gam:jsusta:v:15:y:2023:i:19:p:14091-:d:1245905#:~:text=contributions%20ofNBS,NB%20S%20BMC%20can%20be). The resulting NB S BMC consists of **14 building blocks**​[[econpapers.repec.org]{.underline}](https://econpapers.repec.org/RePEc:gam:jsusta:v:15:y:2023:i:19:p:14091-:d:1245905#:~:text=NBSs%20implemented%20in%20the%20proGIreg,of%20their%20location%20and%20content), expanding the original canvas to capture NBS’s multi-faceted value. This canvas explicitly differentiates between **“value created”** and **“value captured”** for different stakeholders. For instance, centrally it still has the **Value Proposition** (the core benefits of the NBS) and a **Governance** block (who manages and who is involved in decision-making). On the right side (value capture side) it defines **Target Groups** in two categories – **Customers** (those who pay for a service) and **Beneficiaries** (those who benefit but may not pay). This distinction is crucial for NBS like MD DEMO: e.g., anglers or tourists might be paying customers, but the broader community enjoying improved biodiversity are beneficiaries. The NB S BMC also adds four finance-related blocks at the bottom: **Revenue Streams** and **Financing** (distinguishing direct revenues from public or grant funding), and **Cost Structure** and **Cost Reduction** (recognizing that NBS often rely on cost-saving innovations or in-kind contributions). At the top, it adds blocks for **Wider Impacts**: explicitly noting **Positive Societal & Environmental impacts** and any **Negative impacts/risks**. By widening to 14 blocks, the proGIreg canvas captures elements often **missing in a traditional BMC**, such as justifications for public funding (by showcasing public value), and the involvement of stakeholders beyond customers. This model is highly relevant methodology for MD DEMO: it provides a ready template to articulate how a Green Hatchery delivers biodiversity improvements (a public good) and perhaps attracts government or NGO funding, while also creating a product or service (e.g. juveniles for fisheries or educational tours) that generates private revenue. In parallel, a regenerative tourism initiative can use this canvas to map tourist offerings (value proposition), paying visitors (customers), local community who benefit (beneficiaries), partners like conservation NGOs (key partners), required resources (key resources), and blended finance (mix of ticket sales and conservation grants in revenue/financing). In summary, the proGIreg NB S BMC is a **comprehensive, NBS-specific framework** that MD DEMO can adopt to ensure its business model accounts for both traditional business logic and the mission-driven aspects (environmental and social benefits).
